claim: CNGK channels are present in several genomes, primarily in marine invertebrates, yet absent in the genomes of vertebrates such as birds, amphibians, and mammals, except freshwater fish and coelacanths.
source: In several genomes, we identified genes encoding putative cyclic nucleotide-gated K+ channels (CNGK) (Figure 1A). CNGK channels are primarily present in marine invertebrates, yet absent in the genomes of vertebrates such as birds, amphibians, and mammals, except freshwater fish and coelacanths.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1A and stated in the text.

claim: The CNGKs of freshwater fish appear to form a phylogenetic sub-group on their own.
source: The CNGKs of freshwater fish appear to form a phylogenetic sub-group on their own (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic tree analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CNGK channels feature a chimeric structure with a four-repeat pseudotetrameric architecture reminiscent of voltage-dependent Nav and Cav channels.
source: CNGK channels feature a chimeric structure. Their overall four-repeat pseudotetrameric architecture is reminiscent of voltage-dependent Nav and Cav channels, whereas the pore carries the canonical GYG or GFG motif of K+-selective channels (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 1B and sequence analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The pore of CNGK channels carries the canonical GYG or GFG motif of K+-selective channels.
source: Their overall four-repeat pseudotetrameric architecture is reminiscent of voltage-dependent Nav and Cav channels, whereas the pore carries the canonical GYG or GFG motif of K+-selective channels (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: CNGK channels are phylogenetic cousins of cyclic nucleotide-gated (CNG) channels and of hyperpolarization-activated and cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels.
source: Furthermore, CNGK channels are phylogenetic cousins of cyclic nucleotide-gated (CNG) channels and of hyperpolarization-activated and cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels (Figure 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Each of the four repeats of CNGK channels harbours a cyclic nucleotide-binding domain (CNBD).
source: each of the four repeats harbours a cyclic nucleotide-binding domain (CNBD) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The CNGK channel of sea urchin sperm is activated at nanomolar cGMP concentrations.
source: In fact, the CNGK channel of sea urchin sperm is activated at nanomolar cGMP concentrations (Bönigk et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Voltage steps from a holding potential of -65 mV evoked slightly inwardly rectifying currents in whole D. rerio sperm.
source: Voltage steps from a holding potential of -65 mV evoked slightly inwardly rectifying currents (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The reversal potential (Vrev) shifted from -77 ± 3 mV (n = 18) at 5.4 mM extracellular [K+]o to -7 ± 1 mV (n = 7) at 140 mM [K+]o (△Vrev = 51 ± 3 mV/log [K+], n = 7).
source: The reversal potential (Vrev) shifted from -77 ± 3 mV (n = 18) at 5.4 mM extracellular [K+]o to -7 ± 1 mV (n = 7) at 140 mM [K+]o (△Vrev = 51 ± 3 mV/log [K+], n = 7) (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Changing the intracellular [Cl-] did not affect Vrev.
source: Changing the intracellular [Cl-] did not affect Vrev (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: The current in D. rerio sperm is predominantly carried by K+ ions.
source: These results demonstrate that the current is predominantly carried by K+ ions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the K+ dependence of reversal potential and lack of Cl- dependence.

claim: Head and whole-sperm currents displayed a similar K+ dependence (△Vrev = 52 ± 2 mV/log [K+], n = 6).
source: Head and whole-sperm currents displayed a similar K+ dependence (△Vrev = 52 ± 2 mV/log [K+], n = 6) (Figure 1D)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The underlying K+ channel is primarily located in the head of D. rerio sperm.
source: Head and whole-sperm currents displayed a similar K+ dependence (△Vrev = 52 ± 2 mV/log [K+], n = 6) (Figure 1D), rectification (Figure 1F,G), and amplitude (Figure 1F,G), suggesting that the underlying K+ channel is primarily located in the head.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the similarity of currents in isolated heads and whole sperm.

claim: Ion channels involved in sperm signalling are usually localized to the flagellum.
source: This result is unexpected, as ion channels involved in sperm signalling are usually localized to the flagellum.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about sperm ion channel localization.

claim: The anti-HA-tag and the anti-flag-tag antibody labelled proteins of the same apparent molecular mass (Mw) (174 ± 4 kDa (n = 13) and 175 ± 4 kDa (n = 3), respectively).
source: In Western blots, the anti-HA-tag and the anti-flag-tag antibody labelled proteins of the same apparent molecular mass (Mw) (174 ± 4 kDa (n = 13) and 175 ± 4 kDa (n = 3), respectively) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The Mw of DrCNGK is smaller than the predicted Mw of 244.4 kDa.
source: The Mw is smaller than the predicted Mw of 244.4 kDa.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of observed and predicted molecular weights.

claim: The 175-kDa band represents the full-length DrCNGK protein that displays an abnormal electrophoretic mobility similar to other CNG channels.
source: Because flag-tag and HA-tag antibodies recognized the N- and C-terminal end of the CNGK protein, respectively, we conclude that the 175-kDa band represents the full-length protein that, however, displays an abnormal electrophoretic mobility similar to other CNG channels (Körschen et al., 1995; 1999).
evidence: The claim is inferred from antibody recognition of both termini and cited references about CNG channel mobility.

claim: Both anti-repeat1 and anti-repeat3 antibodies labelled membrane proteins of about 170 kDa in Western blots of DrCNGK-expressing CHOK1 cells, D. rerio testis, and sperm, but not of heart, brain, ovaries, and eyes.
source: Both antibodies labelled membrane proteins of about 170 kDa in Western blots of DrCNGK-expressing CHOK1 cells, D. rerio testis, and sperm, but not of heart, brain, ovaries, and eyes (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: 7, 23, 18, and 15 proteotypic DrCNGK peptides were identified by mass spectrometry in testis, mature whole sperm, isolated heads, and isolated flagella, respectively.
source: To scrutinize the antibody specificity, we analyzed by mass spectrometry the ~170-kDa protein band from testis, mature whole sperm, isolated heads, and isolated flagella; 7, 23, 18, and 15 proteotypic DrCNGK peptides were identified, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—source data 1,2).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: Peptides identified by mass spectrometry covered almost the entire DrCNGK polypeptide sequence.
source: Peptides covered almost the entire polypeptide sequence (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The anti-repeat1 antibody labelled structures, most likely sperm, in the lumen of testicular compartments.
source: The anti-repeat1 antibody labelled structures, most likely sperm, in the lumen of testicular compartments (Figure 2D, bottom left).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 2D.

claim: An antisense RNA probe stained sperm precursor cells, in particular spermatocytes, but almost no primary or secondary spermatogonia.
source: An antisense RNA probe stained sperm precursor cells, in particular spermatocytes (Figure 2D, bottom right), but almost no primary or secondary spermatogonia.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The anti-repeat1 and anti-repeat3 antibodies intensely labelled the head and, to a lesser extent, the flagellum of single sperm cells.
source: Finally, the anti-repeat1 and anti-repeat3 antibodies intensely labelled the head and, to a lesser extent, the flagellum of single sperm cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In Western blots of isolated heads and flagella, the DrCNGK was readily identified in head preparations, yet was barely detectable in flagella preparations.
source: In Western blots of isolated heads and flagella, the DrCNGK was readily identified in head preparations, yet was barely detectable in flagella preparations (Figure 2F, n = 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The CNGK channel is located primarily in the head of mature D. rerio sperm.
source: In summary, the CNGK channel is located primarily in the head of mature D. rerio sperm.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including immunocytochemistry, Western blots, and electrophysiology.

claim: The sea urchin ApCNGK channel is opened by cyclic nucleotides and mediates the chemoattractant-induced hyperpolarization.
source: The sea urchin ApCNGK channel is opened by cyclic nucleotides and mediates the chemoattractant-induced hyperpolarization (Bönigk et al., 2009; Strünker et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: Patch-clamp recordings of K+ currents from D. rerio sperm required no cyclic nucleotides in the pipette.
source: Unexpectedly, patch-clamp recordings of K+ currents from D. rerio sperm required no cyclic nucleotides in the pipette (Figure 1C-G).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1C-G.

claim: Mean current amplitudes were similar in controls and in the presence of either cAMP or cGMP (100 µM) in the pipette solution.
source: Mean current amplitudes were similar in controls and in the presence of either cAMP or cGMP (100 µM) in the pipette solution (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Photo-release of cAMP or cGMP from caged precursors did not affect K+ currents in D. rerio sperm.
source: Photo-release of cAMP or cGMP from caged precursors did not affect K+ currents, suggesting that cyclic nucleotides do not modulate DrCNGK (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The photo-release of cAMP or cGMP induced a rapid current increase in heterologously expressed cyclic nucleotide-gated channels ApCNGK from sea urchin.
source: In contrast, the photo-release of cAMP or cGMP induced a rapid current increase in heterologously expressed cyclic nucleotide-gated channels ApCNGK from sea urchin (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The current-voltage (IV) relation, K+ dependence, and block by external TEA of heterologously expressed DrCNGK in X. laevis oocytes was similar to that of the K+ current recorded from D. rerio sperm.
source: We also heterologously expressed the DrCNGK channel in X. laevis oocytes. The current-voltage (IV) relation (Figure 3C–F), K+ dependence (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D), and block by external TEA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F) was similar to that of the K+ current recorded from D. rerio sperm.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 3C–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Currents in oocytes expressing DrCNGK were insensitive to the membrane-permeable analogs 8Br-cAMP and 8Br-cGMP.
source: Moreover, currents in oocytes were also insensitive to the membrane-permeable analogs 8Br-cAMP and 8Br-cGMP (Figure 3C–F)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 3C–F.

claim: Perfusion with 8Br-cGMP increased currents in oocytes that express the ApCNGK channel from A. punctulata sperm.
source: whereas perfusion with 8Br-cGMP increased currents in oocytes that express the ApCNGK channel from A. punctulata sperm (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Swimming behaviour, i.e. path curvature and swimming speed, were not altered by photo-release of cAMP or cGMP in D. rerio sperm.
source: Swimming behaviour, i.e. path curvature (Figure 3H) and swimming speed (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A) were not altered by photo-release
evidence: The claim is supported by motility analysis shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Neither cAMP nor cGMP play a major role in the control of D. rerio sperm motility.
source: In conclusion, we observe no action of cyclic nucleotides on the DrCNGK channel and on the swimming behaviour of D. rerio sperm.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of effect of cyclic nucleotides on currents and motility.

claim: Currents carried by sea urchin ApCNGK show much stronger rectification compared to zebrafish DrCNGK.
source: We noticed a much stronger rectification of currents carried by sea urchin ApCNGK compared to zebrafish DrCNGK (Figure 4A)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Neither Mg2+ nor spermine affected ApCNGK rectification.
source: In classical K+ channels, block by intracellular Mg2+ (Matsuda et al., 1987) or spermine (Fakler et al., 1995) produces inward rectification. However, neither Mg2+ nor spermine affected ApCNGK rectification (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Intracellular Na+ blocked outward currents in ApCNGK in a strong voltage- and dose-dependent fashion.
source: Instead, intracellular Na+ blocked outward currents in a strong voltage- and dose-dependent fashion (Figure 4B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 4B,D.

claim: In the absence of Na+, the IV relation of ApCNGK and DrCNGK channels converged.
source: In the absence of Na+, the IV relation of ApCNGK and DrCNGK channels converged (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: In three of the four ApCNGK pore motifs, a Thr residue is present that in most K+ channels is replaced by a Val or Ile residue.
source: We searched the pore regions of CNGK channels for clues regarding the molecular basis of the Na+ block. In three of the four ApCNGK pore motifs, we identified a Thr residue that in most K+ channels is replaced by a Val or Ile residue (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When Thr residues in the ApCNGK pore were changed to Val, the strong rectification of the mutant ApCNGK channel was lost and the IV relation became similar to that of the DrCNGK channel.
source: When these Thr residues were changed to Val, the strong rectification of the mutant ApCNGK channel was lost and the IV relation became similar to that of the DrCNGK channel (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements of mutant channels shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The Thr residues are absent in CNGKs of freshwater organisms yet present in seawater organisms except for the sponge AqCNGK.
source: Of note, the Thr residues are absent in CNGKs of freshwater organisms yet present in seawater organisms except for the sponge AqCNGK (Figure 4C)
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The different CNGK pores represent adaptations to vastly different ionic milieus.
source: suggesting that the different CNGK pores represent adaptations to vastly different ionic milieus.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between pore residues and habitat.

claim: Intracellular pH (pHi) is an important factor controlling sperm motility in marine invertebrates and mammals.
source: Intracellular pH (pHi) is an important factor controlling sperm motility in marine invertebrates and mammals (Alavi and Cosson, 2005; Dziewulska and Domagala, 2013; Hirohashi et al., 2013; Lishko et al., 2010; Lishko and Kirichok, 2010; Nishigaki et al., 2014; Santi et al., 1998; Seifert et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: In mouse sperm, the Slo3 channels and the CatSper channels are exquisitely pH-sensitive.
source: Moreover, in mouse sperm, the Slo3 channels and the CatSper channels are exquisitely pH-sensitive (Kirichok et al., 2006; Schreiber et al., 1998; Zeng et al., 2011; 2013; Zhang et al., 2006a; 2006b).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: At pHi 6.4, almost no CNGK current was recorded from D. rerio sperm.
source: At pHi 6.4, almost no CNGK current was recorded from D. rerio sperm (Figure 5A, left panel, B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 5A, B, C.

claim: The K+ current in sperm at pH 7.4 with a free Ca2+ concentration of 1 µM was still large, indicating that protons and not Ca2+ are responsible for current inhibition.
source: To rule out that an increase of Ca2+ (from 91 pM to 7.7 nM, see Materials and methods) due to the reduced buffering capacity of EGTA at pH 6.4 is responsible for current inhibition, we recorded sperm currents at pH 7.4 with a free Ca2+ concentration of 1 µM (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). Under these conditions, the K+ current in sperm was still large, indicating that protons and not Ca2+, at least for the concentrations tested, are responsible for current inhibition.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Exposing sperm to 10 mM NH4Cl rapidly elevates pHi.
source: Exposing sperm to 10 mM NH4Cl rapidly elevates pHi (Figure 5G), because NH4Cl overcomes the buffer capacity of HEPES at pH 6.4 (Boron and De Weer, 1976; Seifert et al., 2015; Strünker et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by pH measurements shown in Figure 5G and cited references.

claim: Alkaline pHi strongly enhanced CNGK currents.
source: Alkaline pHi strongly enhanced CNGK currents (Figure 5A, middle panel, B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 5A, B, C.

claim: Subsequent superfusion with 10 mM propionic acid, which lowers pHi, completely reversed the NH4Cl-induced CNGK currents.
source: Subsequent superfusion with 10 mM propionic acid, which lowers pHi, completely reversed the NH4Cl-induced CNGK currents (Figure 5A, right panel, B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 5A, B, C.

claim: 1 mM NH4Cl activated approximately 40% of the CNGK current; at 10 mM, the current was maximal.
source: The NH4Cl action was very pronounced: 1 mM activated approximately 40% of the CNGK current; at 10 mM, the current was maximal (Figure 5D, triangles).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The CNGK current is half-maximally activated at pH 7.08.
source: To quantitatively determine the pH dependence, we recorded sperm K+ currents at different intracellular pHi values (Figure 5C,D circles). The current is half-maximally activated at pH 7.08.
evidence: The claim is supported by pH-response measurements shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: At an NH4Cl concentration of 1.5 mM, pHi in sperm will increase from 6.4 to 7.08.
source: The pH dependence allows to calibrate the NH4Cl action by superposing the data of the two different experimental conditions (Figure 5D): For example, at an NH4Cl concentration of 1.5 mM, pHi in sperm will increase from 6.4 to 7.08 (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the calibration of NH4Cl action against pH dependence shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Alkalization of D. rerio sperm with 10 mM NH4Cl evoked a rapid and reversible hyperpolarization from -49 ± 7 mV to -71 ± 4 mV.
source: Under current-clamp conditions, alkalization of D. rerio sperm with 10 mM NH4Cl evoked a rapid and reversible hyperpolarization from -49 ± 7 mV to -71 ± 4 mV (Figure 5E, n = 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by current-clamp measurements shown in Figure 5E.

claim: 1 mM NH4Cl reversibly increased DrCNGK currents in Xenopus oocytes by approximately 71%.
source: We also studied the pH regulation of the DrCNGK channel expressed in Xenopus oocytes. Oocytes were first perfused with a K+ bicarbonate solution, followed by a K+ gluconate-based solution including 1 mM NH4Cl (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). 1 mM NH4Cl reversibly increased DrCNGK currents by approximately 71%, demonstrating regulation by pHi (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reducing the osmolarity by ~50% does not significantly change DrCNGK currents in oocytes.
source: Furthermore, we tested, whether DrCNGK channels in oocytes are activated by hypoosmotic conditions. Reducing the osmolarity by ~50% does not significantly change DrCNGK currents in oocytes (Figure 5—figure supplement 3, n = 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: In sea urchin sperm, CNGK-mediated hyperpolarization leads to an increase of intracellular Ca2+.
source: In sea urchin sperm, CNGK-mediated hyperpolarization leads to an increase of intracellular Ca2+.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about sea urchin sperm signaling.

claim: Mixing of D. rerio sperm with 10 or 30 mM NH4Cl gave rise to a rapid Ca2+ signal.
source: Therefore, we tested, whether the NH4Cl-induced hyperpolarization (Figure 5E) and alkalization (Figure 5G) evokes a Ca2+ response. In fact, mixing of D. rerio  sperm with 10 or 30 mM NH4Cl gave rise to a rapid Ca2+ signal (Figure 5H, n = 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging measurements shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The time course of the pHi- and Ca2+ signal was similar, suggesting that the CNGK-mediated hyperpolarization triggers a Ca2+ influx.
source: The time course of the pHi- and Ca2+ signal was similar, suggesting that the CNGK-mediated hyperpolarization triggers a Ca2+ influx.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the temporal correlation of pH and Ca2+ signals.

claim: DrCNGK represents a pH-sensitive channel that is strongly activated at alkaline pHi.
source: We conclude that DrCNGK represents a pH-sensitive channel that is strongly activated at alkaline pHi
evidence: The claim is inferred from the pH-dependence of channel activation.

claim: The CNGK-mediated hyperpolarization in D. rerio sperm produces a Ca2+ signal, like in sea urchin sperm.
source: the ensuing hyperpolarization, like in sea urchin sperm, produces a Ca2+ signal.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between hyperpolarization and Ca2+ signal.

claim: Unstimulated D. rerio sperm swam on curvilinear trajectories of low curvature.
source: Unstimulated sperm swam on curvilinear trajectories of low curvature (Figure 6A-F, green segment, Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by motility analysis shown in Figure 6A-F and Video 1.

claim: A UV flash almost instantaneously increased path curvature in NP-EGTA-loaded sperm, but not in control sperm.
source: A UV flash almost instantaneously increased path curvature in NP-EGTA-loaded sperm (Figure 6D-F,I), but not in control sperm (Figure 6A-C,I)
evidence: The claim is supported by motility analysis shown in Figure 6A-F,I.

claim: After Ca2+ release, sperm swam on much narrower arcs.
source: sperm swam on much narrower arcs (Figure 6D-F, red segment, Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by motility analysis shown in Figure 6D-F and Video 1.

claim: The increase of path curvature was even more pronounced after a second UV flash.
source: The increase of path curvature was even more pronounced after a second UV flash (Figure 6 D-F, cyan segment, I, Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by motility analysis shown in Figure 6D-F,I and Video 1.

claim: Many cells were pushing against the wall of the observation chamber and performed a 'spinning' or 'drilling' behaviour, as if to penetrate the wall.
source: Many cells were pushing against the wall of the observation chamber and performed a 'spinning' or 'drilling' behaviour, as if to penetrate the wall (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by motility analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The asymmetry of the flagellar beat increased with each consecutive photo-release of Ca2+ and eventually the flagellum pointed away from the glass surface.
source: The asymmetry of the flagellar beat increased with each consecutive photo-release of Ca2+ and eventually the flagellum pointed away from the glass surface (Figure 6H, Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by motility analysis shown in Figure 6H and Video 1.

claim: This swimming behaviour likely represents a strategy followed by sperm on its search for the micropyle.
source: This swimming behaviour likely represents a strategy followed by sperm on its search for the micropyle, a small opening (outer diameter about 8 µm in diameter) (Hart and Danovan, 1983) on the surface of the much larger egg (about 0.75 mm in diameter) (Selman et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observed behavior and cited references about egg structure.

claim: A similar swimming behaviour during fertilization has been reported for sperm of herring and black flounder.
source: A similar swimming behaviour during fertilization has been reported for sperm of herring and black flounder (Cherr et al., 2008; Yanagimachi et al., 1992; 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: The spinning or drilling movements observed after Ca2+ release reflect the swimming behaviour in vivo down the narrow micropyle.
source: We propose that the spinning or drilling movements observed after Ca2+ release reflect the swimming behaviour in vivo down the narrow micropyle.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposed based on the observed behavior.

claim: Sperm channel orthologues employ different activation mechanisms and serve different functions.
source: A picture is emerging of sperm channel orthologues that employ different activation mechanisms and serve different functions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of CNGK channels across species.

claim: The channel inventories probably reflect adaptations to species-specific challenges during fertilization.
source: The channel inventories probably reflect adaptations to species-specific challenges during fertilization.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observed differences in channel properties.

claim: Calcium in the flagellum controls sperm navigation.
source: Calcium in the flagellum controls sperm navigation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about sperm physiology.

claim: In sperm of marine invertebrates and mammals, Ca2+ signalling has been intensely studied, whereas for fish little is known.
source: In sperm of marine invertebrates and mammals, Ca2+ signalling has been intensely studied, whereas for fish little is known.
evidence: The claim is based on a review of the literature.

claim: In sea urchin sperm, a cyclic nucleotide-gated K+ channel (CNGK) mediates a cGMP-induced hyperpolarization that evokes Ca2+ influx.
source: In sea urchin sperm, a cyclic nucleotide-gated K+ channel (CNGK) mediates a cGMP-induced hyperpolarization that evokes Ca2+ influx.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about sea urchin sperm signaling.

claim: The DrCNGK channel in D. rerio sperm is located in the sperm head rather than the flagellum.
source: It is located in the sperm head rather than the flagellum
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including immunocytochemistry and electrophysiology.

claim: The DrCNGK channel is controlled by intracellular pH, but not cyclic nucleotides.
source: and is controlled by intracellular pH, but not cyclic nucleotides.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: Alkalization hyperpolarizes D. rerio sperm and produces Ca2+ entry.
source: Alkalization hyperpolarizes sperm and produces Ca2+ entry.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological and Ca2+ imaging measurements.

claim: Ca2+ induces spinning-like swimming in D. rerio sperm, different from swimming of sperm from other species.
source: Ca2+ induces spinning-like swimming, different from swimming of sperm from other species.
evidence: The claim is supported by motility analysis.

claim: The 'spinning' mode probably guides sperm into the micropyle, a narrow entrance on the surface of fish eggs.
source: The "spinning" mode probably guides sperm into the micropyle, a narrow entrance on the surface of fish eggs.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observed behavior.

claim: From invertebrates to mammals, sperm use various sensing mechanisms, including chemotaxis, rheotaxis, and thermotaxis, to gather physical or chemical cues to spot the egg.
source: From invertebrates to mammals, sperm use various sensing mechanisms, including chemotaxis, rheotaxis, and thermotaxis, to gather physical or chemical cues to spot the egg.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about sperm navigation.

claim: These sensory cues activate various cellular signalling pathways that ultimately control the intracellular Ca2+ concentration ([Ca2+]i) and, thereby, the flagellar beat and swimming behaviours.
source: These sensory cues activate various cellular signalling pathways that ultimately control the intracellular Ca2+ concentration ([Ca2+]i) and, thereby, the flagellar beat and swimming behaviours (Alvarez et al., 2012; Darszon et al., 2008; Eisenbach and Giojalas, 2006; Florman et al., 2008; Guerrero et al., 2010; Ho and Suarez, 2001; Kaupp et al., 2008; Publicover et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: In species as phylogenetically distant as sea urchin and mammals, signalling pathways target a sperm-specific, voltage-dependent Ca2+ channel, called CatSper.
source: In species as phylogenetically distant as sea urchin and mammals, these pathways target a sperm-specific, voltage-dependent Ca2+ channel, called CatSper.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about sperm Ca2+ channels.

claim: Signalling events open CatSper by shifting its voltage-dependence to permissive, more negative Vm values.
source: Signalling events open CatSper by shifting its voltage-dependence to permissive, more negative Vm values.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about CatSper regulation.

claim: In sea urchin sperm, opening of a K+-selective cyclic nucleotide-gated channel (CNGK) causes a transient hyperpolarization.
source: In sea urchin sperm, opening of a K+-selective cyclic nucleotide-gated channel (CNGK) causes a transient hyperpolarization (Bönigk et al., 2009; Strünker et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: The hyperpolarization in sea urchin sperm activates a sperm-specific Na+/H+ exchanger (sNHE) resulting in a long-lasting alkalization that shifts the voltage dependence of CatSper and leads to a Ca2+ influx.
source: the hyperpolarization activates a sperm-specific Na+/H+ exchanger (sNHE) (Lee, 1984, 1985; Lee and Garbers, 1986) resulting in a long-lasting alkalization that shifts the voltage dependence of CatSper and leads to a Ca2+ influx (Kaupp et al., 2003; Seifert et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: In human sperm, the shift in CatSper voltage dependence is achieved by direct stimulation of CatSper with prostaglandins and progesterone in the seminal fluid or the oviduct.
source: By contrast, in human sperm, the shift is achieved by direct stimulation of CatSper with prostaglandins and progesterone in the seminal fluid or the oviduct (Brenker et al., 2012; Lishko et al., 2011; Smith et al., 2013; Strünker et al., 2011).
